Photograph: EPA Russia ‘Massive’ Ukrainian drone attack on Russia kills at least six, says Moscow Kyiv launches what may be its largest attack wave of war, with fire breaking out at warehouse near Russian capital Dan Sabbagh in Kyiv Sun 16 Aug 2026 07.04 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 08.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukraine has launched one of its largest drone attacks since the start of the war, causing a fire at a distribution warehouse near Moscow and killing at least six people overnight, according to Russian authorities. Russia’s defence ministry said it had shot down 822 drones, while the mayor of Moscow, Sergei Sobyanin, reported that 600 drones were launched towards the capital’s region, of which 201 were destroyed. It was the biggest air raid on the Russian capital in two years, the mayor told the Tass news agency, although the rapid recent expansion of Ukraine’s drone’s capability could mean it was the largest attack wave since the start of the war in 2022. Russian drone missile attacks killed seven people in Ukraine, including two in the central city of Kryvyi Rih, while a Spanish F-18 jet shot down what appeared to be a Russia drone that had crossed the border into Romania. View image in fullscreen Firefighters work to put out a fire at a book market in Kyiv on Sunday. Photograph: Dan Bashakov/AP The Spanish fighter was part of a Nato patrol mission and shot down the drone at about 5am after it crossed into Romanian airspace. “The drone appears to be Russian,” a Nato military spokesperson said. A warehouse belonging to the Russian distribution company Wildberries was set on fire in Podolsk, south of Moscow, with photographs showing a blaze apparently engulfing the 200,000 sq metre warehouse and black smoke extending into the sky. Andrey Vorobyov, the governor of the Moscow region, said the assault was “one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory” – and the Russian defence ministry said later that it had shot down nine Ukrainian cruise missiles and 1,478 drones in the previous 24 hours, though the figure could not be independently verified. Ukraine has rapidly expanded its long-range, deep-strike missile and drone capabilities in 2026, allowing it to attack warehouses, oil refineries, ports and military facilities at distances of up to 1,500 miles (2,400km) from its border. That has allowed Ukraine to nearly match the long-range strike capability that Russia has had since the beginning of the war, at a time when both sides’ air defences are stretched to the point of near exhaustion. Over the past month, Kyiv has shifted focus to attacking facilities linked to the Wildberries company, used widely by businesses to support online retail. Ukrainian attacks have struck about 20 warehouses and buildings in an effort to hurt the Russian economy and affect ordinary citizens financially. Five people were reported to have been killed in Russia’s southern Rostov region, which borders Ukraine. Its governor said a further 150 incoming drones had been destroyed. One person was reported dead in the attacks on the Moscow area. Russian attacks on Ukraine also killed two in the Sumy border region and three others across the country. A ballistic missile attack on Kyiv shortly before 3am injured six and caused several fires in the capital. Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv faces missile barrage after Zelenskyy targets Russian satellite network Read more Fire caused by the attacks destroyed a large part of the Petrovka book market in the Obolonskyi district in Kyiv overnight, with some booksellers reporting they had lost their entire stock in the blaze. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, praised the work of the country’s emergency services and accused the Russians of attacking ordinary people. “Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure,” he said in a social media posting. Over the past week, Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs, and 62 missiles at Ukrainian cities and communities, most of them ballistic missiles of various types. Though Ukraine is effective at stopping slower-moving drones, it has little to no defence against high-speed ballistics, its stock of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles – the only weapons capable of knocking them out – having been run down. https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/20/ed-s.text: Ed Sheeran opened a concert on Saturday with comments about Gaza after controversy swirled around his tour and supporting acts withdrew in solidarity with opener Macklemore, who was dropped after making pro-Palestinian comments onstage at an earlier show.Sheeran began the concert alone on stage with no opener, but was joined by other musicians later in the show.Sheeran said he wants his music and shows to be about unity and humanity, not politics. But he said that while the attacks in Israel of 7 October, 2023, were horrific, what is happening in Gaza “catastrophic and unjustifiable” and slammed it as “disproportionate”.“I don’t want to disappoint fans, and I’ve never wanted to be an activist musician, but this has put me in the middle of an important and passionate argument about freedom of speech and the most complex political issue on the planet,” said Sheeran during his performance at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia.The comments before a nearly full stadium came after a tumultuous week that began with rapper Macklemore, Sheeran's original US opener, being dropped in response to saying “Free Palestine” during a 5 September tour stop in New Jersey.Sheeran has said he was not responsible for the decision, which came at the urging of New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft. His company owns a stadium where Sheeran’s tour was scheduled to play on Friday. Within hours of Sheeran’s statement Tuesday, his supporting acts withdrew.Sheeran has performed many songs solo during his Loop Tour concerts, but was joined for several songs at each stop by the Irish folk band Beoga before they dropped out in support of Macklemore.Macklemore was replaced by Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe before they backed out, and Finneas, Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, was due to tour with Sheeran in South America later this year before he too dropped out this week.Before Saturday's show, a small group of pro-Palestinian demonstrators convened outside the stadium.Hillary Steinberg, 34, said she got concert tickets a year ago but wound up getting a refund and attended the demonstration instead, after she was disappointed that Sheeran refused to take a stand to defend Macklemore or empathise with the plight of the Palestinian people.“I was, until this week, a big Ed Sheeran fan,” Steinberg said. “I think all art is political, and all music is political, and so this choice — even though he was saying that he wasn’t complicit — is a political choice.”Diane Savitz, a 53-year-old from Stroudsburg, Pennsylvania, got tickets months ago and attended. She said she is a big Sheeran fan, doesn't think he did anything wrong and a concert is not the place for politics.“A concert should be for people enjoying the music. Music should bring people together,” Savitz said. “Everyone has their right to freedom of speech, but not every platform is the place for it.”The Grammy winning artist was adamant earlier this week that he wouldn't be drawn into discussion of the war in Gaza, arguing that his fans don’t come to his shows to hear about these issues. But, as the controversy grew, and ticket prices and sales declined, he decided to address the issue head on.Sheeran told the crowd in Philadelphia that everyone is welcome at his concerts, and they can have opposing points of view while still singing his songs, which are about “love, hope and unity.”He also told fans he worries about venues pre-approving performances.“This happens in so many places that I perform around the world, but it should never happen in the free world,” Sheeran said.

https://katv.com/community/little-rock-a.text: A little “Witam”, that’s Polish for hello, is a pretty good way to kick off a weekend that’s all about food, music and community in Central Arkansas. The 36th annual Polish Karnawal is happening this weekend at Immaculate Heart of Mary Catholic School and parish in North Little Rock, with organizers Alisa Tubbs and Brenda Hiegel, inviting the public to come hungry and stay awhile. The event started as a school fundraiser, and it’s still doing that job decades later. Brenda Hiegel, principal of Immaculate Heart of Mary Catholic School, said families at Immaculate Heart of Mary School created the Karnawal as a way to raise money for the school, and “all proceeds go to our school.” She said it’s a joint effort between the parish and the school and has grown beyond the school community into a large local event. A big draw is the traditional Polish dinner on Friday. Doors open at 4:30 p.m., and Alisa Tubbs, development director of Immaculate Heart of Mary Catholic School, recommend arriving early. Dinner costs $18 per adult, and kids 6 and under eat free. The menu includes traditional Polish food: "pierogies, Polish spaghetti, lots of sausage, potatoes”, along with kid-friendly options like chicken fingers. She also highlighted homemade desserts, and food is available while supplies last. The Karnawal also leans into the area’s Polish roots. Hiegel said the community connected to the church and school is called Marche, and the parish and school are approaching a major milestone: “Our church and school are 150 years old in two years.” She said the parish was established by Polish immigrants and that the event helps keep that heritage alive. Beyond the dinner, the weekend includes live music both nights, a midway, concessions, games and bingo. Tubbs described it as a family-friendly event where people bring lawn chairs, listen to bands and reconnect with friends they may only see at the Karnawal each year. The Polish Karnawal is set for Sept. 18 and 19, with the midway open from 5 to 10 p.m. Organizers expect thousands of people and plenty of food, games and activities for kids. Tubbs summed up the plan for the weekend: “It’ll be hot, but the drinks will be cold, so bring a chair and come ready to have some fun.” Organizers also said the beer is Polish from Chicago.

https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/c5x2vw.text: Surgeon having lunch near Krakow shooting undoubtedly saved officer's life, colleague says 8 November 2026 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Olivia Ireland and Nathan Williams Watch: Doctor who treated victims of Krakow shooting speaks to the BBC One of two surgeons who treated victims on the streets in the aftermath of a mass shooting in Krakow, Poland said his colleague "undoubtedly" saved the life of a gravely injured police officer. The pair were eating near the city's Main Market Square on Saturday when a gunman began firing at random, killing six people and injuring 15. The doctors raced to treat both the attacker and two officers shot while subduing the perpetrator. On Sunday, the officers - both hailed as "true heroes" by the prime minister for preventing further deaths - emerged from comas. Prosecutors launched a terror investigation after ministers previously said the 24-year-old Polish attacker - who remains in a critical condition - was apparently inspired by "far-right ideologies". A British national and Austrian woman were among those killed alongside four Poles. Professor Michal Pędziwiatr was having lunch with a colleague, named by local media as Dr Mateusz Wierdak, and their families in central Krakow when they heard gunshots. Pędziwiatr told the BBC: "We saw the shooting attack. And what a surgeon can do in a situation like this?... We decided to help the victims as soon as possible. "We rushed into the area where the shooting was and started our rescue, because there were no ambulances available, there were no professionals around." What we know about the deadly Krakow shooting He said his colleague used his hand to stem the bleeding from the most injured policeman, allowing them to wait for an ambulance which transferred the officer to hospital. Pędziwiatr said they came to learn that one of those they treated was the apparent attacker. "As a doctor... it doesn't matter to me if it's a victim or a suspect," he said. "It's not our task to decide what to do with this guy... for us, it was another heavily injured victim, that's all." According to local media, Wierdak is a renowned surgeon in Krakow. The University Hospital in Krakow states Pędziwiatr is head of General, Oncological, Metabolic and Emergency Surgery. The police officers have been identified as senior constables Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański. Getty Images The attacker has not yet been named by authorities. When his house was searched after the attack in central Krakow, the bodies of his parents and sister were found. The National Public Prosecutor's Office in Poland launched an investigation into the attack with a unit specialising in "terrorist offences" taking the lead. Separately, reports emerged that six Dublin Civil Defence volunteers also assisted in the aftermath of the shooting. Reuters Investigations continued in central Krakow on Sunday before Main Market Square reopened James McConnell, an officer, told RTE News the group were on a city break and were close to the main square when the shooting happened. The volunteers who are trained to provide medical care immediately sought to help injured people, providing "CPR and haemorrhage control". Witnesses who were close to the attack described panic and confusion around the square as it unfolded. Ruby Catherine Warren, from London, heard gunfire and "yelled at my friends to run and we all sprinted for our lives". Not knowing where the gunman was - or if there was more than one - they "just kept sprinting", eventually finding a hotel to hide inside. How the deadly shooting in Krakow unfolded Tom Brook, from West Yorkshire, was inside a McDonald's near the square when he heard "multiple gunshots and saw people running for cover". "I then walked into the square and saw paramedics working on someone outside [a shop] and there was a dead body covered in foil blankets 20 meters away," he said. The suspect wore full military tactical gear during the attack and was described as having a military-grade weapon - but the government said he was not a member of the Polish armed forces. Poland's Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said "everything suggests" the suspect was "fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held ultra-nationalist views. The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) on Saturday in the historic centre of Krakow. Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out. The glass fronts of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes. The mayor of Krakow said he had submitted an urgent request for the two officers injured while stopping the attacker to be awarded titles of honorary citizens of the city. Main Market Square reopened on Sunday evening after a security cordon was lifted.
